source_reviews.independent_solution: At the point of incidence the incident ray, reflected ray and local surface normal are coplanar. The incident and reflected rays lie on opposite sides of the normal, and their angles measured from that normal are equal. The normal to a spherical surface passes through its center of curvature. Angles measured from the surface are complementary to the normal angles, not the incidence/reflection angles.

For a concave spherical mirror in the paraxial approximation, rays incident parallel to the principal axis are reflected through a point on that axis, the real principal focus. For a convex spherical mirror the reflected rays diverge and their backward extensions meet at the virtual principal focus behind the mirror. The focus is not the center of curvature, the vertex or an arbitrary point in the focal plane. In the paraxial spherical model its distance from the vertex is half the radius of curvature.

Four convenient rays in the illustrated concave paraxial construction are: through the center of curvature (AOC), returning along COA; through the focus (AFK), reflected parallel to the principal axis; to the vertex (AP), reflected symmetrically about that axis; and parallel to the principal axis (AE), reflected through the focus along EFA_1. Two distinct applicable reflected ray paths locate A_1; the other applicable rays meet the same image point in the stated model. A central hole removes rays that strike the hole, not every usable reflecting ray. Construct the image from rays hitting the reflecting surface. Constructing edge-point images suffices for the whole object. The auxiliary-axis construction locates D as the intersection of the focal plane with an axis through O parallel to AC, then gives reflected path CD.
